export_users.description: Generate people and get the service's own CSV, JSON, XML or YAML rendering of them as a file you can download, attach to an email or hand to an import tool. This is the one action that returns the service's own field names rather than the tidied ones the other actions use, because an export is meant to be read by something else, and the one that hands back a file rather than data: 5,000 people is several megabytes, so the file is stored and only its opening lines come back inline. A seed is chosen for you when you do not give one, and reported, so any export without a gender can be produced again. No API key required.
export_users.name: export_users

parameters.description: How many people to put in the file, from 1 to 5,000.
parameters.name: count

parameters.description: How to render the people. CSV is one row each and opens in a spreadsheet, but it is the only format that drops the seed from the file, which is why a seed is always chosen and reported separately. Whichever you pick, the result is a file to download rather than text in the step.
parameters.name: export_format

options.label: CSV: one row per person, for a spreadsheet

parameters.description: Whether to draw only women, only men, or whichever comes up. This cannot be combined with a seed: the service silently ignores the gender whenever a seed is set, so asking for both fails the step rather than quietly returning a mix. For the same reason a draw with a gender cannot be repeated later.
parameters.name: gender

parameters.description: Which countries the people should come from. Choose several and each person is drawn from one of them. Leave empty for all twenty-one. This decides the names, the address format, the phone numbers and the national ID number, but not the portraits, which are the same set for every country. Run 'List nationalities' to see what each one yields.
parameters.name: nationalities

options.label: NZ: New Zealand (no national ID number)

parameters.description: Any text. The same seed returns the same people every time, which is what makes a test fixture worth having. Leave empty and one is chosen and reported back, so a run can be repeated afterwards, unless a gender was chosen. Avoid a seed of exactly 18 characters: that length has a special meaning to the service and is refused here.
parameters.name: seed

parameters.description: Which draw of the seed to take. Page 2 of a seed is a different set of people from page 1, not the next slice of one long list, so pages can overlap and cannot be stitched together into a bigger set. Use it to get more people from the same seed without changing the seed.
parameters.name: page

parameters.description: Which parts of a person to return. Leave empty for all of them. Narrowing this is worth doing for a large batch: the login hashes are the expensive part to generate. The nationality always comes back, whatever is chosen here, and the national ID number brings the name with it, because some countries build the number from the name. Use this or 'Leave out these fields', not both.
parameters.name: include_fields

options.label: Login: username, password, UUID and hashes

parameters.description: Which parts of a person to drop. Leave empty to keep everything. Handy for trimming a batch down to what a fixture actually needs. The name stays for as long as the national ID number does, because some countries build the number from the name. Use this or 'Only these fields', not both.
parameters.name: exclude_fields

options.label: Login: username, password, UUID and hashes

parameters.description: Which kinds of character the passwords may use. Choose several to mix them. Leave empty and the passwords are drawn instead from the service's list of about ten thousand real, commonly used passwords, which is the more realistic fixture for testing a password strength check. The length below only applies when at least one of these is chosen. Where the fields can be chosen, the login must be one of them.
parameters.name: password_charsets

parameters.description: The fewest characters a password may have, from 1 to 64. Set this and the longest to the same number for passwords of one exact length. Only applies when a character set is chosen above.
parameters.name: password_min_length

parameters.description: The most characters a password may have, from 1 to 64. The service silently substitutes its own bounds for anything outside that, so a number out of range fails the step here instead. Only applies when a character set is chosen above.
parameters.name: password_max_length

The name stays for as long as the national ID number does, because some countries build the number from the name. Use this or 'Only these fields', not both.
parameters.name: exclude_fields

options.label: Login: username, password, UUID and hashes

parameters.description: Which kinds of character the passwords may use. Choose several to mix them. Leave empty and the passwords are drawn instead from the service's list of about ten thousand real, commonly used passwords, which is the more realistic fixture for testing a password strength check. The length below only applies when at least one of these is chosen. Where the fields can be chosen, the login must be one of them.
parameters.name: password_charsets

parameters.description: The fewest characters a password may have, from 1 to 64. Set this and the longest to the same number for passwords of one exact length. Only applies when a character set is chosen above.
parameters.name: password_min_length

parameters.description: The most characters a password may have, from 1 to 64. The service silently substitutes its own bounds for anything outside that, so a number out of range fails the step here instead. Only applies when a character set is chosen above.
parameters.name: password_max_length

duplicate_emails.description: How many email addresses repeat one earlier in the batch. Addresses are built from names, so two people with the same name share one.

duplicate_usernames.description: How many usernames repeat one earlier in the batch.

fields.description: The parts of a person each record holds, by the service's names for them: gender, name, location, email, login, registered, dob, phone, cell, id, picture and nat.

gender.description: The gender asked for: female, male or any.

nationalities.description: The nationality codes asked for. Empty means all twenty-one.

page.description: Which draw of the seed this is. Each page is a different set of people, not the next slice of one list.

alphabet_size.description: How many different characters a rule could draw from. 0 for the common list.

charsets.description: The character sets the passwords were built from. Empty for the common list.

max_length.description: The longest a password could be. Applies only to a rule.

min_length.description: The shortest a password could be. Applies only to a rule.

source.description: 'charsets' when the passwords were built to a rule, 'common_list' when they came off the service's list of common real passwords.

seed.description: The seed that repeats this draw: the one given, or the one chosen when none was. Empty when a gender was asked for, because a gender cannot be combined with a seed.

users.description: The people, one flat record each.

items.description: One invented person. Only the fields asked for are present, as listed in 'fields'.

address.description: The whole address on one line, for a label or an email.

age.description: Age in whole years on the day of the request. Everyone is an adult.

cell.description: A mobile number, written the way the person's country writes one.

country.description: The country, in English: always the person's nationality.

date_of_birth.description: Date and time of birth, in ISO 8601 UTC.

email.description: An address at example.com built from the name, which can never receive mail.

full_name.description: First and last name together, without the title.

gender.description: The person's gender: female or male.

id_name.description: The national ID number's scheme, such as SSN, NINO or CPF. Empty for Iran, New Zealand, Turkey and Ukraine, which have none.

id_value.description: The national ID number. Null where the nationality has no scheme.

latitude.description: A latitude, random rather than near the address. Null if the service sent one that is not a number.

longitude.description: A longitude, random rather than near the address. Null if the service sent one that is not a number.

md5.description: MD5 of the password followed by the salt, in hex.

nationality.description: Two-letter code of the country the person is from, such as US.

nationality_name.description: The name of that country, in English.

password.description: The password in plain text: built to the rule asked for, or a common real one when no rule was.

phone.description: A landline number, written the way the person's country writes one.

picture_large.description: The address of a large portrait photo, hosted by the service. Faces repeat past about a hundred people.

picture_medium.description: The address of the same portrait, medium-sized.

picture_thumbnail.description: The address of the same portrait as a thumbnail.

postcode.description: The postcode or ZIP code, always as text so a leading zero survives.

registered_date.description: When the account was registered, in ISO 8601 UTC, between 2002 and 2022.

registered_years.description: Whole years since registration, on the day of the request.

salt.description: Eight random letters and digits the three hashes were made with.

sha1.description: SHA-1 of the password followed by the salt, in hex.

sha256.description: SHA-256 of the password followed by the salt, in hex.

state.description: The state, county, province or region.

street.description: House number and street name together.

timezone_description.description: Places that keep that offset, such as Adelaide, Darwin.

timezone_offset.description: A time zone's offset from UTC, such as +9:30. Random rather than the address's own.

title.description: Mr, Mrs, Ms or Miss, or the local form of one, such as Madame, for some countries.

uuid.description: A random UUID, which makes a good external ID for a test account.

version.description: The version of the service the people came from. It is pinned, so the fields a step reads never change.

warnings.description: Anything worth knowing about this draw that did not stop it: a seed overriding the nationalities, a batch large enough that portraits repeat, or a gender that leaves no seed to repeat the draw with.

list_nationalities.description: List the twenty-one countries this integration can generate people from, with what each one yields: the national ID number it issues, or that it issues none, and what its postcodes look like. Worth reading before building a fixture on the assumption that everyone has an ID number: Iran, New Zealand, Turkey and Ukraine have none. This answers from what the pinned version of the service carries, so it costs no request and always works. No API key required.

nationalities.postcode_format: a UK-style postcode, such as EC1A 1BB

list_nationalities.name: list_nationalities

code.description: The two-letter code to choose it by, such as AU.

country.description: The country's name in English, as an address writes it.

has_national_id.description: Whether people from there come with a national ID number.

id_name.description: The national ID number's scheme there, such as TFN. Empty where there is none.

postcode_format.description: What a postcode from there looks like.

postcode_is_digits_only.description: Whether every postcode from there is digits only.

version.description: The version of the service this list is for.

without_national_id.description: The codes of the nationalities that issue no national ID number.

description: Generate invented people for testing, from a service that has been handing them out free since 2013. A person comes with a name, a gender, an email address, a postal address with coordinates and a time zone, phone and mobile numbers, a date of birth, a login with salted MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, a national ID number and a portrait photo. Ask for one or for five thousand, from any of twenty-one countries, and the names, addresses, phone numbers and ID numbers are written the way that country writes them. Give it a seed and the same people come back every time, which is what makes a test fixture worth keeping. Narrower actions return just names, just addresses, just logins or just passwords, and an export action hands back CSV, JSON, XML or YAML ready to write to a file. Nobody generated here is real and every email address is at example.com, which can never receive mail. Every action reads: nothing here changes anything, at the service or anywhere else. No account or API key required.
